newsitem.title: RUSSIA: New crew en route to Mir on difficult mission.
newsitem.headline: New crew en route to Mir on difficult mission.

text.p: Two relief cosmonauts were blazing through space on Wednesday toward the ailing Mir station to attempt repairs that will determine the ship's future.
"The new crew feels fine. We will work with them until 2 a.m. as they have a lot to do," flight director Vladimir Solovyov told reporters after the launch.

As commander Anatoly Solovyov and flight engineer Pavel Vinogradov prepared for a Thursday rendezvous with Mir after a successful launch on Tuesday evening, the current crew continued repairs on the oxygen generating system that has not worked since last week.
Mission Control outside Moscow broadcast live video of Solovyov and Vinogradov, strapped to their seats in spacesuits as they blasted off into orbit.
Solovyov waved goodbye to the camera as the rocket lifted from the Baikonur cosmodrome in Kazakhstan, and minutes later was shown reading a flight manual.

On board Mir the current crew of two Russians and one American were struggling with their latest onboard problem, using solid fuel oxygen generators called 'candles' as they failed to restart the Elektron oxygen system.
It failed to start last week and several days of work have not resolved the problem, which NASA believes is caused by air bubbles trapped in the system.

Mir's back-up oxygen generator is not available for use because it is located in the Kvant-2 module, which the crew powered down to save energy after the space station collided with its supply ship on June 25, causing a major loss of power.

If Solovyov and Vinogradov succeed in reconnecting cables to the solar panels in the damaged Spektr module -- an effort planned for August 20 -- then they can turn on the Kvant-2 again and use its oxygen system.

"The Mir crew has enough oxygen. The atmosphere inside Mir is better than we have in this room," Solovyov said in the airy Mission Control headquarters. "Cosmonauts can work normally for a long time without the Elektron system."

But the repairs inside Spektr will be risky. Space officials say the module, which is now sealed off from the rest of Mir, could contain dangerous floating chemicals or debris. A puncture in a space suit could mean a swift death.
Solovyov, 49, is a four-time veteran of the Mir space station and has spent a total of 456 days in space. Vinogradov, 43, is a space novice but will lead efforts to repair the ship.
On Wednesday the Mir crew were planning to jettison their Progress cargo ship, which is filled with garbage, flight director Solovyov said. It will eventually fall into the Pacific Ocean.

In addition to carrying out last-minute repairs, current commander Vasily Tsibliyev and engineer Alexander Lazutkin were making preparations to return to Earth after a mission in which they have faced one crisis after another since going into orbit in February.
Igor Goncharov, Mission Control's chief doctor, told reporters that Tsibliyev's recent heart troubles posed no danger during their return on August 14.
"We have no doubt that the commander will carry out a normal landing," he said, adding that the first team of recovery experts had already left for the landing site.
